{"date": "1875-12-11", "headline": "Timing the quarter mile", "summary": "Roosevelt clocks himself over a quarter mile and over 400 yards.", "uncertain": "Misdated in the source parse: Theodore Sr. and Mittie's 22nd anniversary fell on December 22, 1875; only the quarter-mile run belongs here."}
{"date": "1877-12-23", "uncertain": "Misdated in the source parse: the museum's opening and the parents' 24th anniversary both fell on December 22, 1877; this entry belongs to that date."}

{"date": "1878-02-09", "summary": "Summoned by urgent word that his father is gravely ill with a bowel tumor, Roosevelt boards the night train for New York. Theodore Sr., 46, dies late that night, hours before his son can reach him.", "uncertain": "The source gives 1 a.m. on February 10 for the death; standard references date it to the night of February 9, 1878."}

{"date": "1881-07-30", "headline": "On to Zermatt", "summary": "Alice rides and Roosevelt walks from Visp to Zermatt in the company of Charley Alexander, whom he finds a fine companion.", "uncertain": "Misdated in the source: Alice's 20th birthday falls on July 29, 1881; that part of this entry belongs to that date."}

{"date": "1881-08-04", "summary": "Roosevelt leaves the hut at 3:45 a.m., reaches the Matterhorn's summit at seven, and is back in Zermatt by 3:30 p.m., hard and risky going, but he is in top condition.", "uncertain": "Misdated in the source: Edith's 20th birthday falls on August 6, 1881; that part of this entry belongs to that date."}

{"date": "1882-09-27", "headline": "Corinne turns 21", "summary": "Roosevelt's sister Corinne has her 21st birthday.", "uncertain": "The source names no one, but Corinne, born September 27, 1861, is the family member who turned 21 this day."}
{"date": "1883-09-07", "uncertain": "Most accounts place this arrival in the small hours of September 8, 1883; the source logs it under September 7."}

{"date": "1886-11-02", "summary": "Democrat Abram Hewitt wins the mayor's race with 90,552 votes. Labor's Henry George finishes second at 68,110, and Roosevelt runs third with 60,435.", "uncertain": "Source error corrected: Hewitt's total was 90,552, not 70,522."}
{"date": "1887-04-28", "uncertain": "Misdated in the source: Corinne's 5th anniversary falls on April 29, 1887; that part of this entry belongs to that date."}

{"date": "1887-12-31", "uncertain": "Date approximate: the club grew out of a dinner Roosevelt hosted in New York in December 1887 and was formally organized early in 1888; the source's Sagamore Hill setting is doubtful."}
{"date": "1889-10-01", "uncertain": "Elliott Roosevelt Jr. is usually dated to September 29, 1889; the source logs his birth here."}
{"date": "1890-08-07", "uncertain": "Misdated in the source: Edith's 29th birthday falls on August 6, 1890; that part of this entry belongs to that date."}
{"date": "1892-10-26", "uncertain": "Misdated in the source: TR's 34th birthday falls on October 27, 1892; that part of this entry belongs to that date."}
{"date": "1894-01-19", "uncertain": "Misdated in the source: Bamie's 39th birthday falls on January 18, 1894; that part of this entry belongs to that date."}

{"date": "1894-04-06", "headline": "Archie's birth, entered early", "summary": "The chronology logs Archibald Bulloch Roosevelt's birth under this date, and again under April 16, but Archie was born on April 9, 1894. The entry describes a midnight delivery so easy and quiet that Roosevelt has to wake the nurse, Mame; he writes Bamie that Edith suffered less than ever, then brings Alice and Ted in to meet their brother.", "uncertain": "Misdated in the source parse: Archie was born April 9, 1894; this entry belongs to that date."}
{"date": "1894-04-16", "uncertain": "Misdated in the source parse: Archie was born April 9, 1894; this entry belongs to that date."}

{"date": "1896-06-02", "headline": "Doubts about Parker", "summary": "In New York Roosevelt tells Bamie he cannot vouch for Commissioner Parker's honesty with money.", "uncertain": "Misdated: the Marquis de Mores was killed on June 9, 1896; the source logs his death here."}
{"date": "1896-06-09", "uncertain": "The Marquis de Mores, founder of Medora, was killed in North Africa this day; the source places his death on June 2."}
{"date": "1896-10-26", "uncertain": "Misdated in the source: TR's 38th birthday falls on October 27, 1896; that part of this entry belongs to that date."}
{"date": "1897-01-19", "uncertain": "Misdated in the source: Bamie's 42nd birthday falls on January 18, 1897; that part of this entry belongs to that date."}

{"date": "1898-02-15", "summary": "At 9:40 that night the battleship Maine explodes in Havana harbor; 260 of her crew die at once and six more later. The sensational papers clamor for war while much of the country seems unmoved. Roosevelt calls it treachery. He also writes Selous, wishing he could get away, and Edith writes her sister Emily Carow.", "uncertain": "Source gives 262 dead; the usual count is 260 killed that night and six more who died later, 266 in all."}

{"date": "1898-04-23", "headline": "A volunteer cavalry post in sight", "summary": "McKinley asks for 125,000 volunteers to bolster a regular army of about 28,000, among them three regiments of frontier horsemen and crack shots. Roosevelt is in line for second in command of the first of these cavalry regiments, under his friend Leonard Wood.", "uncertain": "Roosevelt was offered the post at this time; he resigned from the Navy and took his commission on May 6, 1898."}

{"date": "1900-04-28", "summary": "Roosevelt travels from Chicago back to Albany.", "uncertain": "Misdated in the source: Corinne's 18th anniversary falls on April 29, 1900; that part of this entry belongs to that date."}

{"date": "1901-09-13", "summary": "On Ted's 14th birthday, Roosevelt and a guide climb Mount Marcy in cold, misty weather while the others turn back. Lunching at Lake Tear of the Clouds, he is handed a telegram at 1:25 p.m.: McKinley is failing. A frantic 50-mile night ride takes him to the North Creek rail station and on toward Albany. By early the next morning McKinley is dead.", "uncertain": "McKinley died at about 2:15 a.m. on September 14, 1901, while Roosevelt was still on the road; his death belongs to that date."}
{"date": "1901-09-14", "uncertain": "The source gives 3:15 p.m. for the oath; most accounts put it at about 3:30 p.m."}

{"date": "1902-02-19", "summary": "Roosevelt has Attorney General Knox announce a federal suit to break up the Northern Securities Company, the railroad holding company that Morgan and Kuhn, Loeb money built out of the Harriman and Hill lines; it will be filed at St. Paul in March. The Schley report is published. Ted falls ill with pneumonia at Groton and Edith hurries north to nurse him.", "uncertain": "Knox announced the suit on February 19; it was filed at St. Paul on March 10, 1902."}

{"date": "1902-10-13", "headline": "Morgan brings a plan to Jackson Place", "summary": "Roosevelt asks General Schofield about having the Army run the mines and receives the Chief Justice and the Supreme Court. That evening J. P. Morgan and Robert Bacon, fresh from talks with Root aboard Morgan's yacht Corsair, call on the President at his temporary quarters on Jackson Place. They agree to push the operators to accept a commission of Roosevelt's choosing, with the threat of Army control of the mines in the background.", "uncertain": "The source puts Roosevelt aboard the Corsair; that meeting was Root's, on October 11. On this date Morgan and Bacon came to Roosevelt in Washington."}

{"date": "1902-10-16", "summary": "Roosevelt names a seven-man commission to settle the coal strike: retired Army engineer General John M. Wilson; Labor Commissioner Carroll Wright; federal Judge George Gray of Delaware; E. E. Clark, head of the railway conductors' union, seated under the label of \"eminent sociologist\"; mining engineer Edward Parker; coal man Thomas Watkins; and Bishop John Spalding. He thanks Morgan and Hanna, explains to Cleveland that the operators would not accept him, and sends Mitchell the names.", "uncertain": "Commissioners' roles corrected: Clark led the railway conductors' union; Gray was a federal judge from Delaware."}

{"date": "1903-02-03", "headline": "Trust-busting package nears passage", "uncertain": "The three measures did not all clear Congress this day; they became law on February 11 (Expedition Act), February 14 (Commerce and Labor) and February 19, 1903 (Elkins Act)."}

{"date": "1905-03-04", "summary": "Roosevelt takes the oath before a record crowd of about half a million, with his whole family looking on, and tells the nation, \"Much has been given us, and much will rightfully be expected from us.\" Cowboys, miners and Rough Riders march in a parade of three and a half hours, and that night he talks it all over with Corinne and Douglas in his room.", "uncertain": "The source misquotes the Inaugural Address; the delivered line reads \"Much has been given us, and much will rightfully be expected from us.\" Check against the printed text before publishing."}

{"date": "1905-06-10", "summary": "Roosevelt and Edith have Pine Knot to themselves. He cooks breakfast and chops firewood while she rests in a hammock, and they fry chickens for supper with biscuits, cornbread, cherries and wild strawberries. Word comes that Japan accepts his call for peace talks; Russia will follow two days later.", "uncertain": "Japan accepted on June 10; Russia's formal acceptance followed on June 12, 1905."}

{"date": "1906-01-27", "headline": "A Gridiron Club evening", "summary": "Roosevelt lunches with Dryden and Governor Stokes, sees C. E. Smith and Overstreet, and goes to the Gridiron Club's dinner at the Willard Hotel. He tells Ted he is glad his Harvard work has improved.", "uncertain": "The source places the muck-rake remarks here; Roosevelt's Gridiron Club muck-rake talk is dated March 17, 1906, and he repeated it in public on April 14."}

{"date": "1906-03-17", "headline": "The muck-rake, first told at the Gridiron", "summary": "Roosevelt meets Admiral Dewey, talks canal matters with Hepburn, and sees the German and French ambassadors. After dining with Speaker Cannon he goes on to the Gridiron Club's dinner at the New Willard, where he first compares a certain breed of journalist to the man with the muck-rake in Pilgrim's Progress. Dr. Rixey calls near midnight.", "uncertain": "This Gridiron dinner is where Roosevelt first compared certain reporters to the man with the muck-rake; the source credits that talk to January 27."}

{"date": "1906-04-14", "headline": "The muck-rake speech goes public", "summary": "Roosevelt lays the cornerstone of the new House Office Building and repeats in public his warning against writers who see only the muck. He calls for federal oversight of interstate corporations, presses Congress to pass the Hepburn bill, and backs a progressive inheritance tax. He also talks Indiana politics with Hemenway and ship subsidies with Taft and Humphrey.", "uncertain": "The source logs Robert Barnwell Roosevelt's death here; he died on June 14, 1906."}

{"date": "1906-04-29", "headline": "A lonely spot tied to Washington", "summary": "Aboard the Sylph, Roosevelt and Edith visit a lonely spot linked to George Washington, then in ruins. At home it is his sister Corinne's 24th wedding anniversary.", "uncertain": "The 24th anniversary is Corinne's (married April 29, 1882), not Roosevelt and Edith's."}
{"date": "1906-06-14", "uncertain": "Roosevelt's uncle Robert Barnwell Roosevelt died this day; the source misplaces his death on April 14."}

{"date": "1906-06-29", "headline": "Hepburn Act signed; Mesa Verde created", "summary": "A landmark day: Roosevelt signs the Hepburn railroad rate act. A Grand Canyon game preserve of nearly 1.5 million acres is authorized, and Platt and Mesa Verde national parks are created. He dines with Will Cowles, Root and Bacon.", "uncertain": "The source swaps signings: the Hepburn Act became law June 29, 1906; the Pure Food and Drug Act and the agricultural appropriation with meat inspection were signed June 30. Panama Canal Act date per the source."}

{"date": "1906-06-30", "headline": "Pure food and meat inspection become law", "summary": "As Congress adjourns, Roosevelt signs the Pure Food and Drug Act and the agricultural appropriation that carries the new meat inspection law, and sends Beveridge the pen used on the meat bill. He also approves a law on shooting in the District that makes three-quarters of it a wildlife refuge, and leaves at midnight for Oyster Bay. Alice and Nick head to Cincinnati before sailing for Europe.", "uncertain": "The source swaps signings: the Hepburn Act was signed June 29; the pure food and meat inspection laws belong to this day."}

{"date": "1908-10-31", "headline": "Art store, oil cases, and talks with Japan", "summary": "Roosevelt stops at Fisher's art store after breakfast and goes over the Standard Oil prosecutions with Frank Kellogg. Talks go on toward what becomes the Root-Takahira Agreement, under which the United States and Japan pledge to respect each other's Pacific holdings.", "uncertain": "The Root-Takahira Agreement was concluded by an exchange of notes on November 30, 1908; at this point it was still under negotiation."}

{"date": "1912-02-21", "summary": "Before the Ohio Legislature Roosevelt delivers \"A Charter of Democracy,\" backing popular recall of judicial decisions, a stand that alarms conservatives and business. Chatting with reporters along the way, he lets it be known that his hat is in the ring. His formal answer to the governors who urged him to run comes three days later.", "uncertain": "The 'hat in the ring' line was an informal remark to reporters; his formal declaration came in his February 24 reply to the governors."}

{"date": "1914-04-06", "headline": "Roosevelt asks to be left behind", "summary": "As the party portages more rapids, Roosevelt urges his companions to go on without him so they can survive. Far away in Bogota, American and Colombian envoys sign a treaty, negotiated under Secretary of State Bryan, that voices regret over the 1903 loss of Panama and promises Colombia $25 million.", "uncertain": "The Colombia treaty was signed at Bogota by the American minister, not in Washington."}
{"date": "1915-04-05", "uncertain": "Misdated in the source: Easter Sunday falls on April 4, 1915; that part of this entry belongs to that date."}

{"date": "1915-04-28", "summary": "Roosevelt testifies about U.S. Steel's 1907 takeover of Tennessee Coal and Iron.", "uncertain": "Misdated in the source: Corinne's 33rd anniversary falls on April 29, 1915; that part of this entry belongs to that date."}
{"date": "1916-08-07", "uncertain": "Misdated in the source: Edith's 55th birthday falls on August 6, 1916; that part of this entry belongs to that date."}

{"date": "1877-03-04", "headline": "A Sunday inauguration day for Hayes", "summary": "March 4 falls on a Sunday this year, so Rutherford B. Hayes, who quietly took the oath at the White House the evening before, holds his public inauguration as the 19th President on Monday. In Cambridge, Roosevelt hears from his brother Elliott, writing from Fort McKavett in Texas about the disputed election.", "uncertain": "The source puts Hayes's swearing-in on this day. He took a private oath in the White House on Saturday, March 3, and the public ceremony was on Monday, March 5, 1877."}

{"date": "1877-05-31", "headline": "Customs probe opens as the bridge takes shape", "summary": "The Jay Commission opens its inquiry into graft at the New York Custom House. Over the East River, the Brooklyn Bridge is nearing its cable-making stage: a first trial wire crossed between the towers on May 29, and spinning of the great cables will begin about two weeks later.", "uncertain": "The source dates the start of cable spinning to this day; bridge histories put the first trial wire on May 29 and the start of spinning in mid-June 1877. The hearing date is as given in the source."}

{"date": "1902-05-10", "headline": "Beef trust suit and a deadline for McKim", "summary": "Attorney General Knox opens the government's case against the beef trust. Roosevelt talks over the Rathbone case with Senator Hanna, receives a visiting English textile commission, and has Owen Wister and John Hay to lunch. He tells architect Charles McKim that speed comes first: the new offices and the family's rooms must be ready by October 1. Word is spreading of the eruption of Mount Pel\u00e9e, which wiped out Saint-Pierre on Martinique two days earlier.", "uncertain": "The source logs the Martinique disaster on this day, but Mount Pel\u00e9e erupted on May 8, 1902. Its toll, put at about 40,000 at the time, is now usually given as roughly 28,000 to 30,000."}

{"date": "1904-03-31", "headline": "Canal money, campaign plans, dinner with Holmes", "summary": "Roosevelt goes over canal finances with Attorney General Knox and the coming Republican campaign with Senator Quay, then dines with Justice Oliver Wendell Holmes. Across the Atlantic, Britain and France are closing in on the Entente Cordiale, trading a free French hand in Morocco for British control in Egypt.", "uncertain": "The source places the Anglo-French agreement on this day; the Entente Cordiale was signed in London on April 8, 1904."}

{"date": "1908-06-30", "headline": "Taft steps down from the War Department", "summary": "Taft's resignation as Secretary of War takes effect so he can run his campaign full time, and four troops of cavalry head for the Mexican border. At Sagamore Hill, Roosevelt sits for the sculptor Victor D. Brenner and writes Navy Secretary Metcalf about flaws in American ship design. Half a world away, an enormous blast flattens the forest near the Tunguska River in Siberia.", "uncertain": "The source also logs Bryan's nomination here; the Democratic convention in Denver nominated him on July 10, 1908."}
{"date": "1908-07-27", "headline": "Tennis and talk of Bryan", "summary": "Roosevelt and Archie Butt play tennis and talk over William Jennings Bryan's campaign."}

{"date": "1908-08-05", "headline": "Word of Senator Allison's death", "summary": "News arrives that Iowa's Senator William B. Allison died the day before. Architect C. Grant LaFarge stays the night, and Roosevelt asks Henry Fairfield Osborn for a standard natural history reference so he can study up on African wildlife.", "uncertain": "Senator Allison died August 4, 1908; the source logs his death on August 5."}

{"date": "1913-07-14", "headline": "Archie reaches the canyon rim", "summary": "Archie comes in from Flagstaff by train, bringing Jesse Cummings of Mesa to cook, pack and wrangle for the trip. Roosevelt and Quentin spend part of the day on horseback near El Tovar. Edith writes Kermit that the coming Brazil journey worries her.", "uncertain": "The source runs this day together with the descent into the canyon, which came on July 15, 1913 (Nicholas Roosevelt's account, as summarized by Harvey Leake)."}

{"date": "1913-07-15", "headline": "Down into the Grand Canyon", "summary": "After an early hotel breakfast, Roosevelt, Archie, Quentin, cousin Nicholas and Jesse Cummings ride mules down the Bright Angel Trail and finish the steepest pitch on foot. Rain turns to a thunderstorm as they ride a hand-pulled cable car over the Colorado. A Bar Z hand named Stevenson lends horses for the climb north, and supper by the river is bacon, flat pancakes and canned peas.", "uncertain": "The source logs the descent with July 14; it is placed here from Nicholas Roosevelt's account as summarized by Harvey Leake."}

{"create": "1913-08-24", "date": "1913-08-24", "events": [{"action": "travel", "detail": "On the train from Gallup toward Chicago", "people": ["Archibald Roosevelt", "Quentin Roosevelt", "Nicholas Roosevelt"], "places": [], "time": null}], "headline": "On the train east", "people": [{"name": "Archibald Roosevelt", "role": "family"}, {"name": "Quentin Roosevelt", "role": "family"}, {"name": "Nicholas Roosevelt", "role": "family"}], "summary": "Roosevelt, Archie, Quentin and Nicholas are aboard the train from Gallup, crossing the plains toward Chicago.", "tags": ["travel", "family"], "uncertain": "The source logs the Chicago stop and the return to New York on this day; a Chicago dispatch dated August 26 says he arrived 'yesterday,' and Harvey Leake puts the party back in New York on the 26th."}

{"date": "1913-08-25", "headline": "Sunburned and back in Chicago", "summary": "Burned red by the desert sun, Roosevelt is met in Chicago by a reception committee and a crowd of photographers. He lunches and speaks at the Progressive Club, talks with party leaders, and within a couple of hours boards the Pennsylvania Limited for home.", "uncertain": "The source logs this Chicago stop on August 24; a Chicago dispatch dated August 26 says he arrived 'yesterday.'"}

{"date": "1913-08-26", "headline": "Home from the Southwest", "summary": "The train pulls into New York in the morning. Roosevelt heads straight to the Outlook office to confer with Progressive leaders, meets George McAneny and the fusion candidates at the Harvard Club, and then goes home to Sagamore Hill. He writes Hiram Johnson about California's Progressives, admitting little faith in Wilson, and Frank Dingley about the party in Maine.", "uncertain": "Combines the New York half of the source's August 24 entry, its August 25 Dingley letter and its August 26 McAneny meeting; the letter dates are not independently confirmed."}

{"date": "1915-04-04", "headline": "Easter in a blizzard", "summary": "Easter Sunday finds Sagamore Hill snowbound, the spring storm that hit the day before still blowing. It is also Ethel and Dick Derby's second wedding anniversary."}

{"date": "1915-03-09", "uncertain": "The parse packs several March 1915 entries into single days. The source points to a New York Times list of guests printed March 16, so the Explorers Club luncheon may have been nearer March 15; date not confirmed."}

{"date": "1915-03-15", "uncertain": "The source cites a New York Times story of March 23 for this Flower Show visit, and the parse compresses late March 1915; the visit likely fell nearer March 22. Date not confirmed."}

{"date": "1908-07-28", "headline": "Taft accepts the nomination", "summary": "In Cincinnati, William Howard Taft formally accepts the Republican nomination for president.", "uncertain": "The source logs Taft's acceptance speech on July 27; it was given July 28, 1908."}

{"date": "1898-10-04", "summary": "Leading Republicans travel to Sagamore Hill to formally notify Roosevelt that he is their nominee for governor. His Democratic opponent will be Augustus Van Wyck.", "uncertain": "The source logs Van Wyck's nomination on this day; the Democratic state convention at Syracuse nominated him on September 29, 1898."}

{"date": "1907-11-22", "headline": "Late-night meeting with Morgan on the money crisis", "summary": "After Cabinet and lunch with Henry Taft, Loeb, Justice Harlan, Root and Lodge, Roosevelt meets J. P. Morgan, George F. Baker, Bacon and Cortelyou late into the night on the money crisis. Talks with Tokyo over limiting Japanese immigration, which became the Gentlemen's Agreement, are under way.", "uncertain": "The source says Japan accepted the Gentlemen's Agreement this day; the exchange of notes that made up the agreement ran into early 1908."}

{"date": "1884-10-06", "summary": "At Elkhorn, Sewall and Dow tell Roosevelt of threats against him and his men, of lynchings while he was away, and of the Marquis de Mor\u00e8s's hired gunmen stopping in for a meal. As the story was later told, Roosevelt rode to E. C. Paddock's cabin, told him that if there was to be killing it could start now, and warned him off his men and his claim.", "uncertain": "The confrontation with Paddock comes from later recollections (Sewall, and Hagedorn's Roosevelt in the Bad Lands), not a record made at the time."}
